title: 2,500 Kg of Unsafe Turmeric Seized in Ahmedabad's Madhupura Market
excerpt: Food safety authorities in Ahmedabad seized 2,500 kg of adulterated turmeric from the Old Madhupura spice market, part of a nationwide crackdown after a bride died from contaminated turmeric during a haldi ceremony.
body:
• Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation's food department seized 2,500 kg of adulterated turmeric from the Old Madhupura market area.
  • The crackdown follows a bride's death in Madhya Pradesh's Khargone district after she was exposed to adulterated turmeric during a pre-wedding haldi ceremony.
  • Authorities in Kanpur separately seized 398 kg of adulterated turmeric powder from an industrial area.
  • Common adulterants include lead chromate and metanil yellow — toxic industrial chemicals that survive cooking temperatures.

Food safety authorities in Ahmedabad have seized 2,500 kg of adulterated turmeric from the city's Old Madhupura area, a major wholesale spice market in Gujarat, according to The Times of India.

The seizure is part of a rapid nationwide enforcement response triggered by a deadly incident in Madhya Pradesh, where a bride died during her pre-wedding haldi ceremony after being exposed to adulterated turmeric that caused severe allergic reactions.

The Khargone Tragedy

In Khargone district, Madhya Pradesh, multiple people — including the bride and groom — fell ill shortly after turmeric was applied during the traditional haldi ritual. Red rashes, swelling, and breathing difficulties developed within minutes. Both were rushed to a hospital, where the bride died during treatment.

Preliminary investigations pointed to adulterated turmeric as the cause. The incident sent shockwaves through the country and prompted food safety departments in multiple states to launch targeted raids on spice traders and manufacturers.

Scale of the Ahmedabad Seizure

The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation's food department acted on intelligence gathered during the post-Khargone crackdown. Old Madhupura is one of western India's largest wholesale spice hubs, with hundreds of shops and warehouses dealing in turmeric, chilli powder, coriander, and other staple spices.

"The state government is fully committed to protecting public health, and such strict and deterrent action against adulteration elements will continue in the future as well."

— Praful Pansheriya, Gujarat Health Minister

This is not the first time Madhupura has faced enforcement action. In February 2026, Gujarat's FDCA Food Safety Flying Squad seized approximately 200 kg of loose spices from 30 shops in the same market, citing adulteration risks from unpackaged, unlabeled products.

What Makes Adulterated Turmeric Dangerous

Food safety experts say the most dangerous adulterants used in turmeric are lead chromate — an industrial yellow pigment containing toxic lead and chromium — and metanil yellow, a synthetic dye used in textiles and paper that is banned from food use.

Both chemicals are added to deepen turmeric's yellow color and increase volume at lower cost. Neither is destroyed by cooking, boiling, or roasting, meaning they enter the body through everyday meals.

Long-term consumption can damage the liver, kidneys, and nervous system. Children, the elderly, pregnant women, and those with existing kidney or liver conditions face the highest risk.

A Nationwide Problem

The Ahmedabad seizure coincided with parallel action in Kanpur, where food inspectors seized 398 kg of adulterated turmeric powder from the Chakeri Industrial Area. Across India, the FSSAI has ordered expanded inspections at spice manufacturing units, covering both whole and powdered forms of seven commonly adulterated spices including turmeric, chilli, and cumin.

For Indian households — and diaspora families who regularly import or purchase Indian spices — the incidents are a reminder that whole turmeric, ground at home, remains the safest option. Branded, FSSAI-certified packaged products with clear labeling and expiry dates offer another layer of protection.
nri_angle: Diaspora families who import Indian spices or buy them at South Asian grocery stores should verify FSSAI certification and consider grinding whole turmeric at home for safety.
